nameStory: Yellow Corydalis gets its colorful name from its bright yellow flowers and its Greek roots - 'korydalis' means 'crested lark,' referring to the flower's spurred shape that resembles a lark's crest. It's also called yellow fumewort because early herbalists thought the plant's smoky-blue green foliage looked like rising fumes or smoke.
description: Yellow Corydalis is a delicate herbaceous perennial that grows 6-12 inches tall with feathery, blue-green leaves that look almost fern-like. In spring, it produces clusters of small, bright yellow flowers that have an unusual tubular shape with a distinctive backward-pointing spur. This charming wildflower has a wispy, almost ethereal appearance that makes it look like it's floating above the forest floor.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow tubular flowers with a prominent backward-pointing spur, clustered at stem tips. Each flower is about 1/2 inch long and has an irregular, almost orchid-like shape with a hooded upper petal.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Delicate, finely divided blue-green to gray-green leaves that feel soft and feathery to the touch. The leaves are compound and dissected, giving them a lacy, fern-like appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing plant reaching 6-12 inches tall with multiple branching stems that create a bushy, mounded appearance. The whole plant has an airy, delicate texture.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, narrow seed capsules that split open to release tiny black seeds. The capsules are about 3/4 inch long and hang from thin stalks.

habitat: Yellow Corydalis thrives in open woodlands, rocky slopes, and woodland edges where it gets dappled sunlight. It prefers well-drained, often rocky or sandy soils and is commonly found on hillsides, bluffs, and in clearings within deciduous forests. Look for it in areas that aren't too densely shaded but still have some tree cover.

seasonality.spring: Peak blooming time with bright yellow flowers appearing from April through early June. This is the best time for identification when the distinctive spurred flowers are most visible.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade and seed capsules develop. The feathery foliage remains green but becomes less prominent as surrounding vegetation grows taller.
seasonality.fall: Seeds are dispersed and leaves begin to yellow and die back. The plant becomes increasingly difficult to spot as it goes dormant.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no above-ground parts visible. The plant survives underground as a small rootstock until spring growth begins again.

funFact: Yellow Corydalis flowers are perfectly designed for long-tongued bees - the nectar is stored way back in that distinctive spur, so only bees with tongues long enough to reach it can pollinate the plant, creating an exclusive pollinator partnership!
confusionNotes: With only 5 recorded observations in New England, Yellow Corydalis might be confused with other small yellow spring wildflowers like wild ginger or buttercups, but none of these have the distinctive spurred flower shape or the feathery, blue-green foliage that makes corydalis unique.
contextualKnowledge: Yellow Corydalis is quite rare in New England with only 5 documented observations, making it a special find for nature enthusiasts. It's much more common in the southeastern United States, so any New England sighting could be at the northern edge of its range.
compareHints: Yellow Corydalis differs from its corydalis cousins by its bright yellow flower color - most other corydalis species in our region have pink, purple, or white flowers. Golden Corydalis is similar but typically larger and more robust, while the other corydalis species have completely different flower colors, making Yellow Corydalis fairly easy to distinguish when in bloom.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Bird-in-a-bush differs from other New England Corydalis species mainly in its spring ephemeral nature and tuberous root system.
Golden corydalis is quite rare in New England compared to its relatives, with only 8 recorded observations.

Unlike the more robust Yellow Corydalis with its coarser leaves and bright yellow flowers, incised fumewort has much more finely divided, delicate foliage and typically produces pink to purple blooms.
Noble Corydalis stands out from other New England corydalis species by its larger size, bright golden-yellow flowers (rather than pink, purple, or pale yellow), and more robust growth habit.
Hollowroot differs from other New England corydalis species primarily in its early blooming time and the distinctive hollow tuber (though you shouldn't dig to check this).
Among the Corydalis species, Fern-leaved Corydalis stands out for having the most finely-divided, fern-like foliage - other corydalis have more substantial, less delicate leaves.
